Class Demo 🔍 DNS in Action: The Number That Would Not Load

The Mystery: A Machine That Answers but Will Not Serve

Type ping tiktok.com into a command window. A reply comes back from a number such as 23.34.62.177. That number is an IP address, and the reply proves a machine is alive at that address. Now paste the same number into your browser. The page fails. The name works and the number does not. In this demo you watch the failure happen, and the reason behind it explains how most of the modern web is hosted.

Learning Objectives Supported 🎯

  • 1.2. Describe how IP addresses, DNS, domain names, and the parts of a URL work together to locate a page on the web - CLO I

Run the Demo 🛠️

Work through the steps in order, and make your prediction before you test it. You need a browser and a command window. On Windows, search the Start menu for Command Prompt. On a Mac, open Terminal.

  1. Look up the number. Type ping tiktok.com and press Enter. Write down the IP address in the reply.
  2. Compare. Ask a classmate what number they got. Different numbers are normal here, and Quick Check question 1 asks why.
  3. Predict: Ping reached the machine, so the browser should reach it too. What do you expect to see when you visit http:// plus your number?
  4. Run: Paste http:// followed by your number into the address bar and press Enter. Then try again with https:// in front of the number.
  5. Explain: The HTTP attempt answers with the error 400 Bad Request. The HTTPS attempt fails before any page arrives. Before you read on, write one sentence guessing why a reachable machine refuses to hand over the page.

Key Terminology 🔑

  • content delivery network (CDN): A company that serves copies of many websites from machines placed near visitors.
  • virtual hosting: Many websites sharing one IP address on one server.
  • Host header: The part of every browser request that names the website you want.
  • certificate: The ID card a server shows over HTTPS to prove which site it is.

What Just Happened

The machine you pinged is real, but it is not a TikTok computer.

  • That address belongs to Akamai, a content delivery network. A CDN parks copies of many websites on machines close to visitors, and each of its machines serves thousands of different sites.
  • So the server's first question is: which of my thousands of sites do you want? Your browser answers with the domain name, which rides inside every request in a field called the Host header. Paste a bare number and no name arrives, so the server refuses with 400 Bad Request. Many sites sharing one address this way is called virtual hosting.
  • HTTPS fails even sooner. A certificate proves a site's identity by name, and this machine holds no certificate for a bare number. Your browser gives up before it asks for a page.
  • Picture it this way: an IP address is an office building, and a domain name is the company you ask for at the front desk. Ping only proves the building exists. Walk in without naming a company and the front desk cannot help you.

It Works in Both Directions

DNS is not one name matched to one number. The mapping runs many-to-many, in both directions at once.

  • One name, many numbers. Run the same ping from campus, from home, and from your phone, and you may get three different addresses. DNS hands each visitor a machine near them, which is why your classmate's number differed from yours.
  • One number, many names. The machine you pinged also serves sites that have nothing to do with TikTok.
  • The exception: type https://1.1.1.1 into your browser. It loads, because Cloudflare wrote the bare number into its certificate on purpose. Its service helps people whose DNS is broken, so the number has to work on its own. Almost no other site bothers.
  • Carry forward: ping proves a machine is reachable. Only a name gets you a website.

Quick Check ✅

  1. Your ping of tiktok.com returned a different number than your classmate's, and the site loads fine for both of you. Explain in two sentences why nothing is broken.
  2. Use the office building analogy to explain why http://23.34.62.177 fails while https://www.tiktok.com works.
  3. The address https://1.1.1.1 loads from a bare number. What did Cloudflare do that TikTok did not, and why did Cloudflare need it?

Prove It: Same Machine, Name Attached (Optional) 🧪

Still not convinced the same machine serves the page once it hears the name? The curl tool can attach the name by hand. Run these in Command Prompt or Terminal, and swap in the number from your own ping. On Windows, use Command Prompt for this step, because PowerShell treats curl as a different command.

curl -I http://23.34.62.177/

The reply is 400 Bad Request from a server named AkamaiGHost. Now ask the same machine again, with the domain name riding along:

curl -I https://www.tiktok.com/ --resolve www.tiktok.com:443:23.34.62.177

The reply is HTTP/2 200. Same machine both times. The only difference is that the second request carries the name, so the front desk knows which site to fetch.

Hold on to this idea. In Module 12 you publish your own site, and your hosting company will park it on a shared IP address beside sites you have never heard of. Virtual hosting is the reason hosting costs a few dollars a month instead of the price of a whole server.
